short: manage bare-metal machines through their BMCs (Redfish) and the pk-metal operator that runs in a Kubernetes cluster
long:
exit status:
  0  success
  1  error; the message is on stderr, as "pk-metal: <message>"
  2  pk-metal status only: something is blocked or failed and needs a person

flags.name: context
flags.usage: kubeconfig context to use (default: the current context)

flags.name: kubeconfig
flags.usage: kubeconfig file (default: $KUBECONFIG, then ~/.kube/config, then the in-cluster account)

commands.short: show machines, BMCs, claims and operations, with the reason when something is stuck (reads only)
commands.long:
Tables:
  HOST       one row per machine: its asset, vendor, phase, the claim that
             holds it, the Talos node it runs (name and address), how many of
             its BMC paths answer, and what blocks it
  OPERATION  each operation that has not succeeded: waiting for approval,
             running, or failed (failed ones stay until you retry them)
  ENDPOINT   one row per BMC
  CLAIM      claims that have no machine yet
  CLUSTER    one row per TalosCluster: Talos and Kubernetes versions wanted
             and running, ready control planes and workers, etcd health,
             when it was bootstrapped, the backup state, and whether its
             Kubernetes API is available
  NODE       one row per TalosNode: its cluster, role, the host it runs on,
             address, Talos version, boot stage and readiness
  ROLLOUT    each TalosRollout that has not succeeded: its cluster, kind,
             nodes done of the plan, where it stands (the reason it waits)
             and who approved it
Under each table, every blocked or failed row gets a line that says why, in
the operator's own words, and what to run next when there is a command for it.

-o json prints the same facts as one JSON object, for scripts:
  {"version": 1, "needsAttention": bool,
   "hosts":      [{"name", "asset", "vendor", "phase", "claim",
                   "node": {"name", "address"} or null,
                   "pathsUp", "pathsTotal", "blockedOn", "message", "needsAttention"}],
   "operations": [{"namespace", "name", "host", "phase", "approvedBy",
                   "blockedOn", "message", "needsAttention"}],
   "endpoints":  [{"name", "asset", "vendor", "phase", "address",
                   "blockedOn", "message", "needsAttention"}],
   "claims":     [{"namespace", "name", "asset", "host", "phase",
                   "blockedOn", "message", "onHold", "needsAttention"}],
   "clusters":   [{"name", "talosVersion", "talosVersionsRunning",
                   "kubernetesVersion", "kubernetesVersionRunning",
                   "controlPlanes", "readyControlPlanes", "workers",
                   "readyWorkers", "available", "etcd", "bootstrappedAt",
                   "backup", "backupMessage", "message", "needsAttention"}],
   "nodes":      [{"name", "cluster", "role", "host", "address", "version",
                   "stage", "ready", "message", "needsAttention"}],
   "rollouts":   [{"name", "cluster", "kind", "nodesDone", "nodesTotal",
                   "state", "approvedBy", "message", "needsAttention"}]}
  Every key is always present; a missing value is "" (or null for node).
  "operations", "claims" and "rollouts" list all of them, also succeeded and
  bound ones.
  New keys may be added; existing keys keep their meaning while version is 1.

exit status:
  0  nothing needs a person
  1  error: the cluster could not be read
  2  something is blocked or failed (a row has needsAttention), including
     operations that wait for approval, a bootstrapped cluster whose etcd or
     Kubernetes API is unhealthy or whose backup is stale, a node of a
     running cluster that is not Ready, and a rollout that waits for
     approval, cannot plan, pauses after its first node, or failed
commands.example:
pk-metal status
  watch -n 10 pk-metal status
  pk-metal status -o json | jq '.hosts[] | select(.needsAttention)'

commands.short: say what is wrong with a cluster's etcd and propose the operations that restore it; upload an approved snapshot
commands.long:
restore looks at a cluster's etcd on every control plane and says what is
wrong and what would fix it. It changes nothing on a machine itself: with
--propose it creates the operations of the plan, and each waits for another
person's approval like any other.

The talosconfig is read from the cluster's published Secret
(<cluster>-talosconfig in pk-metal) unless --talosconfig names a file.

https://metal.platform-kit.org/operate/day-2/restore-etcd/ walks through each case.
commands.example:
pk-metal restore plan lab
  pk-metal restore plan lab --snapshot lab-daily-20261124-060000 --propose
  pk-metal approve pk-metal/lab-etcd-recover-node-1          (a person; see selfApproval)
  pk-metal restore upload pk-metal/lab-etcd-recover-node-1 --identity ~/.config/age/keys.txt

flags.name: talosconfig
flags.usage: talosconfig file (default: the cluster's published Secret)

commands.short: say what is wrong with the cluster's etcd and what would fix it; --propose creates the operations
commands.long:
One member lost (its etcd does not run or reports errors while the
others keep their majority): remove that member, wipe the node's etcd
data (EPHEMERAL) and let it join again.
Majority or everything lost (no control plane lists etcd members):
wipe the etcd data of the members that still run a stuck etcd, then
restore one control plane from a snapshot (etcdRecover); the others
join it. The newest verified snapshot is used unless --snapshot names
one.

flags.name: node
flags.usage: control plane to restore on (default: the first by name that answers)

flags.name: propose
flags.usage: create the plan's operations (each waits for approval)

flags.name: snapshot
flags.usage: EtcdSnapshot to restore (default: the cluster's newest verified one)

commands.short: stream the snapshot of an approved etcdRecover operation to its node
commands.long:
For an approved etcdRecover operation: decrypt the snapshot on this
machine with your age identity, check it against the snapshot record,
and stream it to the node over the Talos API with your talosconfig.
The operator then starts etcd from it.

flags.name: from-file
flags.usage: the encrypted snapshot as a file (needed for a pvc sink)

commands.short: see the rollouts that change a Talos cluster node by node (config, upgrade, reboot), approve one, resume it after its pause, or abort it
commands.long:
A rollout changes the nodes of one Talos cluster one at a time: a config
change, a Talos upgrade, a Kubernetes upgrade or a rolling reboot. The
operator proposes rollouts on its own when the cluster spec and the machines
disagree; it never starts one. A person approves the plan.

The approval names the plan by its hash. If the plan changes before the
first node starts (a node was added, the spec changed again), the approval
no longer covers it: the rollout ends as PlanChanged and the operator
proposes a fresh one.

After the first node the rollout always pauses, so you can look at that node
before the rest follow. Control planes go first, one at a time, then workers.
commands.example:
pk-metal rollout list
  pk-metal rollout show lab-talosupgrade-1a2b3c4d
  pk-metal rollout approve lab-talosupgrade-1a2b3c4d
  pk-metal rollout resume lab-talosupgrade-1a2b3c4d

commands.short: every rollout, newest last, with its state
show the plan, ask, and approve exactly that plan

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: do not ask (for scripts); the plan is still printed and still approved only as read

commands.short: stop for good: no further node starts; the node that runs now finishes. An abort cannot be taken back
